toc.title: IV.A.1: Understand the setting in which the AI will be used
IV.A.2: Understand the differences between AI model types
IV.A.3: Understand the differences between deployment options

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Check the setting of an AI use case: goals, performance needs, data, ethics and people
  • Tell apart model types: predictive or generative, closed or open, small or large, text-only or multimodal
  • Tell apart deployment options: cloud, on-premises or edge, and as is, fine-tuned, retrieval-augmented or agentic
  • Spot the risks each choice brings, and who carries them
  • Reach a decision: go, go with conditions, or no-go

2IV.A.1: Understand the setting in which the AI will be used

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

Choosing the Assistant's Model and Setup

  • Anika Berg, the Customer Support director, wants the customer assistant to answer service questions faster
  • Context: the goal is clear, but some support documents are out of date and the support staff need training
  • Model: Helios weighs a large closed model from Corvid Labs against a small open model it could host itself
  • Setup: answer from retrieved support documents or fine-tune the model; an agentic "book a meeting for me" function is held back
  • Samira Haddad asks the question this module answers: go, go with conditions, or no-go?

Start With the Use Case: Five Context Factors

  • Before any model is chosen, define the setting in which the AI will work
  • Goals: the problem, the benefit expected and how success will be measured
  • Performance needs: how accurate, fast, available and explainable it must be
  • Data: what exists, how good it is and whether it may be used
  • Ethics and risk: who could be affected and how much oversight is needed
  • People and skills: who will operate, check and rely on it

Exam tip: The context comes first and the model second: a model chosen before the use case is understood is a guess.

Goals and Performance Needs: What Good Enough Means

  • A clear goal names the problem, the user and the measure of success
  • Performance requirements turn the goal into numbers: accuracy, error tolerance, speed, availability, explainability and cost
  • Tolerance for error follows harm: a wrong film suggestion is cheap; a wrong hiring ranking is not
  • Set thresholds before testing (module 9) and review them if the use changes
  • A need that cannot be measured cannot be shown to be met
  • Helios: the assistant must answer in seconds, in plain language, and say when it does not know

Exam tip: The cost of a wrong output sets the performance bar: higher harm, tighter requirement.

Data Availability: Can the Use Case Be Fed?

  • Every use case runs on data: the system's own and any organization data it draws on
  • Ask four questions: do they exist, are they good enough, may we use them, do they represent real use?
  • Missing or poor data may rule a use case out, or change the approach: collect first, narrow the scope, or use a pre-trained model
  • Rights and privacy: lawful basis, purpose limits and licensing (modules 4 and 5)
  • Helios: the support documents exist, but some are old; fixing them comes before go-live

Exam tip: No suitable data, no suitable use case: say so before money is spent on a model.

Ethics and Risk Appetite: Who Is Affected?

  • Ask who is affected, how seriously, and whether the effect can be undone
  • Rights and fairness: work, credit, health and education set high bars in law and ethics (modules 1, 5 and 6)
  • Human oversight: does a person review the output, or does the system act alone?
  • Risk appetite: the level of risk the organization accepts, set by leaders and the committee
  • More effect and more autonomy mean more governance, and sometimes do not deploy

Exam tip: Weigh effect on people and autonomy together: high on both calls for the strongest controls.

Workforce Readiness and the Go or No-Go Decision

  • People and skills: can staff use the tool, check its output and escalate problems? (module 2 training)
  • Change management: roles shift, so plan communication, support and a feedback route
  • Capacity: who will monitor, maintain and answer questions after launch?
  • The decision: go, go with conditions (for example training first), or no-go
  • Findings feed the model and option choices, then the impact assessment (module 12)
  • Helios: support agents learn when to correct the assistant before launch

Exam tip: A technically sound system still fails if the people around it are not ready.

3IV.A.2: Understand the differences between AI model types

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Classic and Generative Models

  • Classic (predictive) models score, classify or predict, often from structured data: a ranking, a yes or no, a number
  • Generative models create new content: text, images, code or audio
  • Classic: a narrow task and outputs that are easier to measure; generative: broad tasks and open-ended outputs that are harder to test
  • Classic risks: biased scores, opacity, poor data
  • Generative adds: confabulation, harmful content, leakage and intellectual property questions
  • Helios: the hiring tool is predictive; the assistant is generative (module 1)

Exam tip: Open-ended output means open-ended failure modes, so testing and monitoring must be broader.

What Generative AI Adds to the Risk List

  • The NIST generative AI profile names twelve risks unique to or worsened by generative AI (module 1)
  • Content: confabulation, dangerous, violent or hateful content, obscene or abusive content, information integrity
  • Data and rights: data privacy, intellectual property
  • Security: information security, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) information or capabilities
  • People and systems: human-AI configuration, harmful bias or homogenization
  • Supply chain and planet: value chain and component integration, environmental impacts
  • Choosing a generative model means deciding which apply and how each will be controlled

Exam tip: In a generative AI case, expect confabulation, privacy leaks and intellectual property to be in play.

Proprietary and Open-Source Models

  • Proprietary (closed) models: owned by a provider and reached through an interface; internals and training data are usually not visible
  • Open-source or open-weight models: the weights are public, so you can inspect, host and adapt them
  • Closed: provider-managed updates and support, less control; open: control and transparency, but more work for you in hosting, security, testing and updates
  • Licenses differ: open models can carry usage limits; read them
  • Either way, the deployer must evaluate the model for its own use
  • Helios: the Corvid Labs model is closed; an open alternative was weighed

Exam tip: Open does not mean risk-free or rule-free: the deployer carries more of the safety work.

Open Source and the Law

  • AI Act, Article 2(12): systems released under free and open-source licenses are largely outside the Act, unless they are high-risk, prohibited (Article 5) or subject to transparency duties (Article 50)
  • General-purpose models, Article 53(2): open-source providers are exempt from the technical documentation and downstream information duties
  • They still owe the copyright policy and the training-content summary, and the exemption is lost for systemic-risk models (module 6)
  • Article 25(4) supplier agreements do not cover free and open-source components, except general-purpose models
  • GDPR, product liability and other laws apply whatever the license

Exam tip: The open-source exemption is partial: copyright policy and training summary remain, and systemic-risk models never qualify.

Small and Large Models Beyond the BoK

  • Large models: broad abilities and varied tasks, but higher cost per use, slower responses and harder to test fully
  • Small models: narrower, cheaper and faster, able to run on your own hardware or a device; they may need retrieval or fine-tuning to reach quality
  • Fit over size: choose the smallest model that meets the requirements
  • Governance: small models can keep data in-house; the providers of the largest models may face systemic-risk duties (module 6)
  • Test both on your own tasks: public benchmarks may not reflect your use
  • Helios: a small open model could handle routine questions

Exam tip: Bigger is not automatically better or safer: match the size to the task and the risk.

Language and Multimodal Models Beyond the BoK

  • Language models work with text, including code
  • Multimodal models take in or produce images, audio and video as well as text
  • New uses: reading scans and charts, describing images, voice assistants, video analysis
  • New risks: deepfakes and synthetic media (Article 50 transparency, module 6), biometric and sensitive data in faces and voices (module 4), hidden instructions in images, and more ways to attack the system
  • Test each input type and check the data rights for each
  • Helios: the hiring tool's video interview handles voice and video, so sensitive-data and emotion-analysis limits apply (modules 4 and 6)

Exam tip: Every added modality adds questions about data, security and transparency.

Matching the Model Type to the Task

  • Start from the task, not from the technology
  • Rank, classify, predict: classic models
  • Draft, summarize, answer: generative language models
  • Images, audio, video: multimodal models
  • Closed or open, small or large: decide on control needs, cost, data sensitivity and testing
  • Record the reasons in the decision record

Exam tip: Match the model type to the task and the risk, and write down why.

4IV.A.3: Understand the differences between deployment options

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 3 practice questions on this indicator.

Where It Runs: Cloud, On-Premises or Edge

  • Cloud: run on a provider's infrastructure: quick to start, scalable, less to maintain
  • On-premises: run in your own data centers: the most control over data and security, but you buy and run everything
  • Edge: run on the device, such as a phone, camera or vehicle: fast, works offline, data stay local, but limited power and harder updates
  • Hybrid setups mix these
  • Drivers: data sensitivity, speed, cost, skills and laws on data location

Exam tip: Where the system runs decides who controls the data, the security and the updates.

Cloud Deployment: Shared Responsibility and Data Location

  • Shared responsibility: the provider secures the infrastructure; the customer secures its data, access settings and use
  • Data location and transfers: moving personal data across borders must meet the GDPR transfer rules (Articles 44 to 49), so check where the provider processes and stores data (module 4)
  • Contract terms: use of your data for the provider's own training, logging and retention, sub-processors, audit rights, incident notice (module 12)
  • Lock-in and continuity: what happens if the provider changes the model, the price or its service?
  • Concentration risk: too many services on one provider
  • Helios: the assistant reaches its model through a cloud interface, so these terms matter

Exam tip: The cloud moves work to the provider; it does not move the legal responsibility for the data.

On-Premises and Edge: Control, Cost and Maintenance

  • On-premises: data stay inside your boundary, you set security and access, and strict data rules are easier to meet
  • Cost and effort: hardware, specialists, patching, capacity planning and your own monitoring
  • Edge: local processing reduces transfers and delay, useful where the network is poor or the data are sensitive
  • Edge limits: small models, limited power, many devices to update and secure, and physical access risks
  • Updates: a flaw in a model on thousands of devices needs a patch and withdrawal plan
  • Helios: hosting an open model itself would add security and maintenance duties the team does not have today

Exam tip: More control means more work: choose it only when the need justifies the effort.

How the Model Is Used: A Ladder of Adaptation

  • As is: the model with careful prompts and guardrails: least effort, least fit
  • Retrieval-augmented: the model answers using documents fetched at the moment of the question
  • Fine-tuned: the model is trained further on your data to change its behavior
  • Agentic: the model plans steps and uses tools to act
  • Combinations are common; start with the least adaptation that meets the need
  • Each step up adds effort, cost and risk to govern

Exam tip: Try the simplest approach first, and add adaptation only when testing shows a gap.

Using the Model As Is: Prompts, Guardrails and Other Techniques

  • Prompt design: instructions, examples and a system prompt shape behavior without changing the model
  • Guardrails: input and output filters, topic limits, blocked actions and fallbacks to a person
  • Other techniques: parameter settings, caching, combining models, and distillation (a small model trained to imitate a larger one)
  • Limits: the model's knowledge and flaws stay the same, and guardrails can be bypassed by clever inputs
  • Governance: record the prompt and settings as part of the system version, and test them
  • Helios: Anika Berg's team writes the assistant's system prompt: tone, scope and say you do not know

Exam tip: Prompts and settings are part of the system: version, test and review them like code.

Fine-Tuning: Benefits, Risks and Role Changes

  • Fine-tuning: further training on your own examples to change style, format or domain behavior
  • Benefits: better fit, shorter prompts, sometimes a smaller model
  • Risks: leakage of training data in outputs, bias in the new data, drift from the original safety behavior, extra cost, and the need to retest everything
  • Data governance: the fine-tuning data need the same lineage, quality and rights checks as any training data (module 9)
  • Role change: a substantial modification of a high-risk system can make the deployer its provider (Article 25); module 12 returns to this
  • Facts that change often belong in retrieval, not in the weights

Exam tip: Fine-tune for behavior and style; use retrieval for facts that change.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Grounding on Your Documents

  • The system retrieves relevant passages from your documents and gives them to the model with the question
  • Benefits: answers use current company content; update the documents without retraining; sources can be shown
  • It reduces, not removes, confabulation: the model can still misread or ignore a passage
  • Risks: stale or wrong documents (the Helios refund error), access control (users seeing documents they should not), injection through documents, and poor retrieval
  • Governance: owners, review dates and versions for the knowledge source; test retrieval and answers; log the sources used

Exam tip: With retrieval, the document source is part of the system: its quality is the system's quality.

Agentic Architectures: Autonomy and Excessive Agency

  • Agentic systems plan multi-step tasks and use tools, such as calendars, email, payments or code, to act on their own
  • New risk: a mistake or a manipulated instruction becomes a real action, quickly and at scale
  • Excessive agency (OWASP list): more functions, permissions or autonomy than the task needs
  • Controls: least-privilege tools, limits on actions and spending, human approval for consequential steps, logging and a kill switch (module 10)
  • Test for misuse, injection and chains of errors, not only single answers
  • Helios: the "book a meeting for me" function is held back until permissions, approvals and logging are designed and tested

Exam tip: Autonomy multiplies the impact of every other risk: limit it, and keep a person in the loop for consequential actions.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Anika Berg wants the Helios assistant to answer service questions. The goal is clear and the support staff are trained, but the support documents are scattered, out of date and contradict one another. Which factor of the use-case context is the main concern?

  • AWorkforce readiness, because the support staff have not yet been trained to use the new tool in daily work
  • BEthical considerations, because some customers might prefer to speak with a person
  • CData availability and quality, because the information the assistant needs is unreliable
  • DPerformance requirements, because the assistant must answer within a few seconds
Show the answer

Answer: C. The stem says the goal is clear and staff are trained, so the weak point is the data: the documents are old and conflicting. Fix them before go-live, or the assistant will repeat the errors.

S2A claims team plans to use AI to triage insurance claims. Which TWO questions belong in the context review before a model is chosen? (Select TWO.)

  • AWhich vendor has the most attractive website and the longest list of public awards and industry prizes
  • BWhich model on the market has the largest number of parameters
  • CHow many wrong triage decisions the business can tolerate, and what harm each would cause
  • DWhich colors and fonts will appear on the screens that the claims handlers use
  • EWhether the claims handlers have the skills and time to review the output and correct it
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. The context review covers performance needs, including how much error is tolerable, and workforce readiness. Vendor branding, parameter counts and screen design are not context factors.

S3Which statement best describes a difference between proprietary and open-source models?

  • AOpen models give the deployer more control and visibility, and more responsibility for security and testing
  • BProprietary models are always safer, because only the provider can see how they were built and trained in-house
  • COpen-source models are exempt from the law, because their license allows anyone to use them for free or modify them
  • DProprietary models can be adapted by anyone who downloads their weights and runs them locally
Show the answer

Answer: A. Open weights let the deployer inspect, host and adapt the model, and the deployer then owns more of the safety work. Closed models are not automatically safer, open models are not exempt from law, and only open weights can be downloaded and adapted.

S4The Helios assistant mostly answers short, routine questions about services. A colleague proposes always using the largest available model. What is the best governance response?

  • AAgree, because a larger model produces safer, more accurate and fairer answers for most tasks and users
  • BAgree, because model size has no effect on cost, speed or how fully the model can be tested
  • CReject large models, because large models are not able to be combined with a company's own documents or data
  • DTest whether a smaller model meets the requirements, choose the smallest one that does and record why
Show the answer

Answer: D. Fit matters more than size: a smaller model may meet the need at lower cost, with faster answers and easier testing. Test it, choose the smallest that works and record the reasons.

S5A hospital needs an AI tool for dictated patient notes. Its policy says patient data must not leave the hospital network, and the tool must keep working during network outages. Which deployment option fits best?

  • AA public cloud service reached over the internet, because it is the quickest to start
  • BOn-premises or edge deployment, because data stay inside the hospital and no connection is needed
  • CA cloud service in another country, because it lowers cost and the hospital's policy can be changed later on
  • DA hybrid design in which the patient data are first sent to a provider for processing
Show the answer

Answer: B. Keeping data inside the network and working offline point to on-premises or edge deployment. Cloud options send data out and depend on a connection.

S6Which TWO statements about retrieval-augmented generation are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • AIt grounds answers on retrieved documents, so document quality and freshness affect answer quality
  • BIt changes the model's weights by training it further on the organization's own documents
  • CIt removes the risk of wrong answers, because each answer is checked against the documents before it is shown
  • DIt requires the whole model to be trained again from scratch on the organization's own data each time
  • EIt lets an organization update what the system knows by changing the document source, with no retraining
Show the answer

Answer: A, E. Retrieval grounds answers on documents and lets the organization update knowledge by updating them. It does not change the weights (that is fine-tuning), it does not remove errors, and it needs no training from scratch.

S7Helios proposes an assistant function that books meetings for customers: it reads emails, checks calendars and sends invitations on its own. Which feature of this design calls for the most careful governance before deployment?

  • AIt produces much more text than a chat assistant would, so storage cost is the main concern
  • BIt runs in the cloud, and cloud deployments are outside the reach of company policy or contract
  • CIt uses a fine-tuned model, and fine-tuned models are not allowed under the EU AI Act
  • DIt acts with tools and permissions, so mistakes or manipulated instructions have real effects
Show the answer

Answer: D. An agentic function turns errors and manipulated instructions into actions. It needs least-privilege permissions, limits, human approval for consequential steps, logging and a kill switch. The other claims are false or minor.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Context goals, performance needs, data, ethics and risk, people and skills; the outcome is go, go with conditions or no-go
Model types classic or generative; closed or open (the open-source exemptions are partial); small or large (choose the smallest that fits); language or multimodal
Where it runs cloud, on-premises or edge, with who controls data and updates
How it is used as is, retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned or agentic: the least adaptation that works
Watch-outs retrieval depends on the documents, fine-tuning can leak and shift roles, agentic needs limits and approval
